# We found 331 MCP tool-list changes in one week that only moved a date. Each one costs a prompt-cache write

Posted on Nov 3 • Originally published at modelmarket.dev

A reader of our last post, Paul Irolla, who builds a token optimizer for coding agents, pointed out something we had only looked at as a correctness problem. A model request starts with the tool list. Change one byte of a tool definition and every prompt cache built on that request is gone, even if the change means nothing.

HISTOR, our public log of MCP tool definitions, records every change it sees, so we counted. In the week of 25 October to 1 November it recorded 10,712 changes to the tool lists of 4,491 MCP servers. 331 of them changed nothing but a date or a timestamp.

With Anthropic's API, the cached prefix is built in a fixed order: tools first, then the system prompt, then the messages. A change anywhere in the tools invalidates everything after it. Reading a cached prefix costs a tenth of the normal input price. Writing one costs 1.25 times the input price, or twice for the one-hour cache. So the same tool list costs about 12 times more on a miss than on a hit, and so does everything behind it. Other providers discount cached input by different amounts, but the principle is the same: an identical prefix is cheap, a changed one is not.

Inside one session this mostly doesn't bite. Clients fetch tools/list when they connect and keep it until the server says the list changed. It bites between sessions. If you run many agent sessions with the same servers, the cached prefix carries over from one session to the next until a byte changes. A server that rewrites its definitions twice a day resets that for everyone who uses it.

For every change in the week, we took both stored tool lists, the one before and the one after, and compared them tool by tool, ignoring more and more at each step:

The step at which the two lists become equal names the change:

HISTOR's digest sorts tools and keys, so a list that only changed order isn't recorded as a change at all, and doesn't appear here. And HISTOR sees at most one change per read, every 30 minutes to 6 hours. But if the price moves every few hours, the description is a costly place to keep it. Every move resets the cache for every client, including the ones that will never call that tool. A price that floats is better quoted at call time. Paid MCP tools over x402 already get a priced offer in the HTTP 402 answer.

If you maintain an MCP server and want the model to know the date, or how fresh your data is, there are places that don't touch the tool list:

None of this changes what the model can know. It only moves the moving parts out of the one block that every request shares.

If you build a client or a token optimizer, the per-server history is public. HISTOR's changes API, https://histor.modelmarket.dev/api/v1/changes, lists every recorded change with the digests of both sides and a field-by-field diff. A server that changed its definitions seven or more times in a week is a good candidate to fetch once per session and pin. 218 servers did that this week, and between them they made 3,661 changes, a third of the total.

The week's counts, the script and the examples behind this post are at https://histor.modelmarket.dev/datasets/cache-churn-2026-11-01/.

Disclosure: we build HISTOR. AI assistance was used for the analysis, the code and the writing. The counts come from HISTOR's production database, read-only, in a throw-away container.

# Two MCP logs matched 23 tools. Five days later, every name had changed.

Compare the latest saved entries for one MCP server and you get zero tool names in common. Compare the observations from the same evening and all 23 tool fingerprints match. We maintain HISTOR, a transparency log for th

Image: Two MCP logs matched 23 tools. Five days later, every name had changed.

Compare the latest saved entries for one MCP server and you get zero tool names in common. Compare the observations from the same evening and all 23 tool fingerprints match.

We maintain HISTOR, a transparency log for the tool definitions MCP servers advertise. We wanted to see whether an independent observer could corroborate one of our observations. We picked LEGION-tlog because it publishes a timestamp and a SHA-256 fingerprint for each tool. Those fingerprints let us compare individual definitions even when the logs use different formats for their records. LEGION developer documentation

## What the two logs saw

The server was `com.aiapplyd/aiapplyd`. We compared the tool name, description and input schema using LEGION’s canonicalization rule for per-tool fingerprints. All times below are UTC in 2026. HISTOR server history · LEGION server record

HISTOR observation  | What the comparison showed
--- | ---
19 October, 21:37:07  | All 23 fingerprints matched the LEGION observation from 22:01:05, about 24 minutes later.
24 October, 18:19:21  | All 23 names switched from `aiapplyd_` to `getmattered_`. The suffixes matched the earlier names. The latest entry in our archived LEGION response still showed the October 19 observation.
31 October, 12:45:49  | HISTOR recorded a set of 40 tools. None of their names appeared in the archived LEGION record. This is the set in the November 2 HISTOR snapshot.

The October 24 observation is easy to misread if you only look at counts. Both sets contain 23 tools, but a client using the earlier names would have to account for the name changes. The matching suffixes give you a way to line up the names. Whether the tools behave the same would take a separate test.

The evidence tells us when HISTOR first recorded the new set and which earlier version LEGION corroborated. It leaves open why the archived LEGION response had no later entry. In particular, the time of an observation and the time a server actually changed can differ.

## Replay the check offline

Download the offline replay bundle.

With the case bundle unpacked, run this from its directory using Node.js 22.
    
    `node replay.mjs > replay-output.json
    diff -u result.json replay-output.json
    `

An empty diff means the replay reproduced the saved result. The script uses Node’s standard library and the bundled records, keys, signed tree heads (STHs) and inclusion proofs. It performs three checks.

  1. LEGION-tlog. Verify the signing key against the pinned root key, verify the Ed25519 signatures on leaf 29030 and its STH, and recompute the path to the signed root of the 50,578-leaf Merkle tree.
  2. HISTOR. Verify the STH and the three signed MTL/1 labels against HISTOR’s pinned `did:key`. Verify their inclusion in the 1,564,894-leaf Merkle tree and recompute the tool set digest bound to each label.
  3. Comparison. Recompute the per-tool fingerprints from the authenticated HISTOR tool sets and compare them with the fingerprints in the LEGION record. The output lists names unique to either side and any shared names whose definitions differ.

The signed HISTOR label for the 40-tool set dates to October 31. The November 2 read time comes from snapshot metadata. The replay verifies inclusion under the bundled tree heads. Checking consistency across other tree heads or the behavior of the server would require separate evidence.

For a tool-pinning workflow, the case suggests a concrete diagnostic. When two logs disagree, put the observation timestamps next to the fingerprints and look for an earlier matching tool set. That can turn a generic mismatch into a dated, inspectable change.

We maintain HISTOR. AI assistance was used for the analysis, the replay code, the illustrations and the writing.

📰 Read the original article on Dev.to Security

## If your problem is the bill, look at your tool list

Threads are a latency fix. Cache hygiene is where the money is, and the MCP ecosystem is leaking it. HISTOR, a public log of MCP tool definitions, recorded 10,712 changes to the tool lists of 4,491 MCP servers in the week of 25 October to 1 November — and 331 of those changed nothing but a date or a timestamp.

That matters because of prefix ordering: with Anthropic's API the cached prefix is built tools first, then system prompt, then messages, so a change anywhere in the tools invalidates everything after it. By HISTOR's accounting, reading a cached prefix costs a tenth of the normal input price while writing one costs 1.25 times input (twice for the one-hour cache) — roughly 12 times more on a miss than on a hit. A single server was responsible for 237 of the 331 date-only changes.

## What to do next

If you run long agent sessions and your bottleneck is time to first token on huge contexts, threads are worth an afternoon of testing — with your full-history replay path kept intact. If your bottleneck is spend, audit which MCP servers rewrite their definitions daily; HISTOR found 218 servers that changed definitions seven or more times in a week, and pinning those per session is the cheaper fix.
